title: Atomic ironing for conformal interfaces in freestanding oxide nanomembranes
authors: Jeongkeun Song, Keaghan Knight, Keun-Yeol Park, Young-Hoon Kim, Tyler J. Sachs, Hu Miao, Jiaqiang Yan, Celesta S. Chang, Ambrose Seo, Ho Nyung Lee
abstract: Atomically well-defined interfaces are essential for realizing functional interlayer coupling in stacked and twisted oxide heterostructures, yet transferred freestanding oxides can develop structural inhomogeneities, including local curvatures, interfacial voids, and incomplete contacts with substrates. Here, we demonstrate that these transfer-induced structural disorders and imperfections evolve substantially and can be suppressed by post-transfer thermal treatments, yielding bulk-like crystalline freestanding oxide nanomembranes. Using freestanding SrTiO3 membranes as a model system, we report a systematic understanding of the role of "atomic ironing" and the associated evolution of lattice mosaicity, interfacial roughness, and optical bandgap. We further demonstrate atomically bonded conformal interfaces in twisted SrTiO3 heterostructures, highlighting the importance of post-transfer thermal processes. These results establish a synthetic strategy to restore the structural integrity and intrinsic bulk-like functionality of freestanding oxide nanomembranes, enabling stacked, twisted, and heterogeneously integrated oxide architectures with atomically well-defined interfaces for emerging quantum functionalities.
summary: This work demonstrates that structural defects introduced during the transfer of oxide nanomembranes, such as $	ext{SrTiO}_3$, can be systematically repaired using post-transfer thermal annealing, a process termed "atomic ironing." By monitoring structural metrics like mosaicity and roughness via XRD and XRR, the authors prove that annealing restores bulk-like crystalline quality, enabling the creation of atomically perfect interfaces necessary for advanced quantum oxide architectures.
main_problem: Transfer-induced structural disorders and imperfections in freestanding oxide nanomembranes degrade their intrinsic functionality, which is critical for advanced quantum device integration.
main_result: Post-transfer thermal annealing, termed "atomic ironing," successfully restores structural uniformity, reduces lattice mosaicity, and creates atomically conformal interfaces in the oxide membranes.
method: The study uses a sacrificial-layer-based lift-off process to create freestanding $	ext{SrTiO}_3$ membranes, followed by systematic thermal annealing and characterization using XRD, XRR, and STEM.
model_or_system: The physical system is freestanding $	ext{SrTiO}_3$ ($	ext{m-STO}$) oxide nanomembranes, which are fabricated and tested on various substrates, including those used for twisted heterostructures.
key_observables: XRD rocking curve FWHM, XRR interface roughness, lattice mosaicity, optical bandgap, and atomic-scale interface continuity (confirmed by STEM/EDS).
important_parameters: Annealing temperature (ranging from $300^\circ	ext{C}$ to $700^\circ	ext{C}$), substrate type ($	ext{SiO}_2/	ext{Si}$, $	ext{Al}_2	ext{O}_3$), and twist angle ($\phi_{	ext{twist}}$).
main_assumptions: The structural recovery achieved through annealing directly correlates with the restoration of the intrinsic, bulk-like optical functionality of the oxide material.
figures_summary: Figures demonstrate the systematic narrowing of XRD rocking curves and reduction of XRR roughness with increasing annealing temperature, alongside STEM images showing membrane flattening and atomically flat interfaces in twisted structures.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of problem identification (transfer damage) $ightarrow$ methodology (lift-off, annealing, characterization) $ightarrow$ systematic demonstration of structural recovery (XRD/XRR) $ightarrow$ confirmation of functional recovery (optical/STEM) $ightarrow$ establishing a general synthetic strategy.
why_interesting: The ability to engineer interfaces at the atomic scale via thermal treatment is crucial for realizing functional quantum devices, as structural perfection dictates the quality of electronic coupling in heterostructures.
